questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes mechanical processing?
questions.why: Mechanical processing is physical, not chemical — crushing and breaking food into smaller fragments so it moves more easily through the tract. Digestion is the chemical breakdown.

options.t: Food is chemically broken into subunits
options.why: That is digestion.

options.t: Food is crushed into smaller fragments
Nutrients cross into interstitial fluid
options.why: That is absorption.

options.t: Enzymes and buffers are released inward
options.why: That is secretion.

questions.stem: Absorption is defined as which of the following?
questions.why: Absorption is movement across the epithelium into the interstitial fluid. Secretion is the release of substances INTO the tract, and excretion is the removal of waste.

options.t: Waste leaves mixed with indigestible residue
options.why: That is excretion.

options.t: Nutrients cross the lining into the fluid
Food is chemically broken into subunits
options.why: That is digestion.

options.t: Enzymes and salts are released inward
options.why: That is secretion.

questions.stem: What are the six processes the digestive system is responsible for?
questions.why: Ingestion, mechanical processing, digestion, secretion, absorption, excretion. Secretion is the one most often left off the list.

options.t: Ingestion, mechanical processing, digestion, secretion, absorption, and excretion
Mechanical processing, digestion, secretion, absorption, metabolism, and excretion
options.why: Ingestion is missing from this list.

options.t: Ingestion, mastication, digestion, absorption, storage, and excretion
options.why: Secretion and mechanical processing are missing.

options.t: Ingestion, digestion, absorption, metabolism, storage, and elimination
options.why: Secretion is missing from this list.

questions.stem: What is the alimentary canal, and what does it include?
questions.why: The alimentary canal is a series of muscular tubes running mouth to anus — pharynx, esophagus, GI tract, and rectum. The GI tract is only the stomach and intestines portion of it.

options.t: Organs producing digestive enzymes
options.why: Those are the accessory organs.

options.t: Muscular tubes running mouth to anus
The membrane suspending the organs
options.why: That is the peritoneum.

options.t: The stomach and intestines only
options.why: That is the GI tract, a portion of the canal.

questions.stem: Which organs are the accessory digestive organs?
questions.why: The accessory organs produce and secrete enzymes and juices essential to digestion. They are not part of the GI tract structure itself but aid in digestion.

options.t: Stomach, small and large intestine
options.why: Those form the GI tract itself.

options.t: Pharynx, esophagus, and duodenum
options.why: Those are alimentary canal structures.

options.t: Esophagus, stomach, and the rectum
options.why: Those are alimentary canal structures.

options.t: Teeth, tongue, glands, liver, pancreas

questions.stem: Which layer of the alimentary canal wall carries out secretion and absorption?
questions.why: The mucosa — surface epithelium, underlying connective tissue, and a small amount of smooth muscle — carries out secretion and absorption. The submucosa nourishes surrounding tissues and carries away absorbed materials.

options.t: The serosa
options.why: That protects and secretes lubricating fluid.

options.t: The mucosa
The muscular layer
options.why: That produces the movements of the tube.

options.t: The submucosa
options.why: That nourishes tissue and carries absorbed material away.

questions.stem: The muscular layer is made of two smooth muscle coats. What does each do?
questions.why: Circular fibers encircle the tube and cause contraction; longitudinal fibers run lengthwise and shorten the tube. Together they produce the movements of the canal.

options.t: Both run lengthwise, alternating action
options.why: One coat is circular and one longitudinal.

options.t: Circular shorten; longitudinal squeeze
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Circular squeeze; longitudinal shorten
Inner secretes mucus; outer contracts
options.why: Mucus comes from the mucosa, not the muscle layer.

questions.stem: What does the serosa do?
questions.why: The serosa is composed of visceral peritoneum on the outside with connective tissue beneath. It protects underlying tissues and secretes serous fluid so the abdominal organs slide freely.

options.t: Absorbs nutrients into the tissue fluid
options.why: That is the mucosa's role.

options.t: Protects and secretes lubricating fluid
Produces the movements of the tube
options.why: That is the muscular layer's role.

options.t: Carries absorbed material into the blood
options.why: That is the submucosa's role.

questions.stem: Which organs are found in the right upper quadrant?
questions.why: RUQ holds the liver and gallbladder plus some colon and small intestine. The stomach and spleen are LUQ.

options.t: Cecum and appendix
options.why: Those are in the right lower quadrant.

options.t: Descending colon only
options.why: That is in the left lower quadrant.

options.t: Liver and gallbladder
Stomach and spleen
options.why: Those are in the left upper quadrant.

questions.stem: A patient presents with pain in the right lower quadrant. Which structures are located there?
questions.why: RLQ contains the cecum, ascending colon, and appendix — which is why RLQ pain raises suspicion for appendicitis. The LLQ holds the descending and sigmoid colon.

options.t: Descending and sigmoid colon
options.why: Those are in the left lower quadrant.

options.t: Liver, gallbladder, and duodenum
options.why: Those are in the right upper quadrant.

options.t: Cecum, ascending colon, appendix
Stomach, spleen, and pancreas
options.why: Those are in the left upper quadrant.

questions.stem: What is the peritoneum, and what is the difference between intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal organs?
questions.why: The peritoneum is a large, moist, continuous sheet of serous membrane covering most intra-abdominal structures. Organs sit either inside it (intraperitoneal) or behind it (retroperitoneal).

options.t: A serous sheet; organs sit in or behind it
A vessel network; organs drain into it or not
options.why: It carries vessels but is not a vessel network.

options.t: A muscle wall; organs sit above or below it
options.why: The peritoneum is a serous membrane, not muscle.

options.t: A fat layer; organs attach to or float free
options.why: It is a serous sheet, not adipose tissue.

questions.stem: What is the mesentery, and what does it contain?
questions.why: Mesentery is folds of peritoneum that suspend the abdominal organs within the cavity, and it carries nerves, arteries, veins, and lymph vessels.

options.t: Connective tissue joining liver to diaphragm
options.why: That is a ligamentous attachment.

options.t: A muscular sheet dividing chest from abdomen
options.why: That is the diaphragm.

options.t: Peritoneal folds carrying vessels and nerves
The outer serous covering of the intestine
options.why: That is the serosa.

questions.stem: What is the role of the soft palate?
questions.why: The hard palate is the bony plate lying anteriorly. The soft palate is a fold of mucous membrane and muscle extending posteriorly into the throat, designed to hold food being chewed and help initiate swallowing.

options.t: Closes the airway during normal breathing
options.why: The epiglottis protects the airway.

options.t: Grinds food against the surface of the tongue
options.why: That is the hard palate's role.

options.t: Holds chewed food and starts swallowing
Supports the tongue from the mouth floor
options.why: The floor of the mouth supports the tongue.

questions.stem: How many teeth of each type are in a single quadrant?
questions.why: Each of the four quadrants has one central incisor, one lateral incisor, one canine, two premolars, and three molars. The front teeth mainly tear or cut the food.

options.t: Two incisors, one canine, two premolars, three molars
One incisor, one canine, three premolars, three molars
options.why: There are two premolars, not three.

options.t: Two incisors, two canines, two premolars, two molars
options.why: There is one canine per quadrant, and three molars.

options.t: Two incisors, one canine, one premolar, four molars
options.why: There are three molars, not four.

questions.stem: The salivary glands are composed of serous cells and mucous cells. What does each secrete and do?
questions.why: Serous cells produce amylase, which starts digesting starchy food right in the mouth. Mucous cells produce mucus, which binds and lubricates items in the mouth.

options.t: Serous make acid; mucous make buffer
options.why: Neither cell type secretes acid.

options.t: Both make amylase at differing strengths
options.why: Only serous cells produce amylase.

options.t: Serous make amylase; mucous make mucus
Serous make mucus; mucous make amylase
options.why: The two are reversed here.

questions.stem: What are the dimensions of the esophagus, and what is its key limitation?
questions.why: The esophagus is a hollow, collapsible tube about 10 inches (25 cm) long surrounded by smooth muscle. It transports food from mouth to stomach but cannot absorb nutrients.

options.t: About 10 inches; it cannot absorb
About 5 feet; it absorbs only water
options.why: The esophagus is far shorter than that.

options.t: About 10 inches; it absorbs nutrients
options.why: It transports but cannot absorb nutrients.

options.t: About 20 feet; a major absorption site
options.why: That describes the small intestine.

questions.stem: What is peristalsis, and what does it accomplish in the esophagus?
questions.why: Peristalsis is a series of wavelike contractions propelling food into the stomach — which is why swallowing works even lying down or upside down.

options.t: One sustained squeeze forcing food down
options.why: Peristalsis is a repeating wave, not one squeeze.

options.t: Relaxation letting food fall by gravity
options.why: Swallowing works against gravity.

options.t: Mixing motion that produces chyme
options.why: That describes stomach churning.

options.t: Wavelike contractions pushing food down

questions.stem: What is the function of the portal vein?
questions.why: The portal vein is formed by a complex series of converging veins and transports venous blood from the GI tract to the liver, where absorbed nutrients are processed.

options.t: Carrying oxygenated blood to the gut
options.why: Arteries carry oxygenated blood to the gut.

options.t: Draining the liver into the right atrium
options.why: The hepatic veins drain the liver.

options.t: Returning intestinal lymph to the blood
options.why: Lymph returns through the thoracic duct.

options.t: Carrying gut blood to the liver

questions.stem: Where is the stomach located, and what protects it?
questions.why: The stomach is a hollow organ in the left upper quadrant, mostly protected by the lower left ribs.

options.t: Right upper quadrant, under the liver
options.why: That is where the liver sits.

options.t: Midline above the navel, unprotected
options.why: It sits to the left rather than the midline.

options.t: Left upper quadrant, under the ribs
Left lower quadrant, at the pelvic brim
options.why: The stomach sits in the upper abdomen.

questions.stem: What is the principal function of the stomach?
questions.why: The stomach receives food in large quantities intermittently, stores it, and provides for its movement into the small intestine in small amounts. The largest part is the body, which stores undigested food and liquid.

options.t: Neutralize acid before the intestine
options.why: Neutralization happens in the duodenum.

options.t: Store food and release it gradually
Absorb the majority of digested nutrients
options.why: That is the small intestine's role.

options.t: Complete the reabsorption of water
options.why: That is the large intestine's role.

questions.stem: What is chyme, and how does it leave the stomach?
questions.why: Muscular contractions in the stomach wall plus gastric juice convert food into chyme, a mixed semisolid mass. It is expelled through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.

options.t: A solid mass passing straight to the jejunum
options.why: Chyme is semisolid and passes through the duodenum first.

options.t: An absorbed solution entering the portal vein
options.why: Absorption happens in the intestine, not the stomach.

options.t: A semisolid mass, out through the pylorus
A thin liquid, back through the cardiac valve
options.why: Chyme moves forward, not back into the esophagus.

questions.stem: What proportion of the products of digestion does the small intestine absorb, and where does it send them?
questions.why: The small intestine absorbs more than 90% of the products of digestion into the veins for transport to the liver.

options.t: About 75%, sent into the lymphatic system
options.why: That understates it, and absorption goes to the veins.

options.t: About 50%, sent directly to the heart
options.why: That understates small intestine absorption.

options.t: Over 90%, sent onward to the liver
Under 25%, with the rest absorbed in the colon
options.why: That greatly understates its role.

questions.stem: What is the role of the duodenum?
questions.why: The duodenum receives food from the stomach — the pylorus acts as the valve between them — and connects the pancreas, liver, and gallbladder to the digestive system.

options.t: Completes the reabsorption of water
options.why: That is the large intestine.

options.t: Prepares chyme for the large intestine
options.why: That is the ileum.

options.t: Serves as the main absorptive segment
options.why: That is the jejunum.

options.t: Receives chyme and the accessory ducts

questions.stem: What are the specific roles of the jejunum and the ileum?
questions.why: Jejunum absorbs, ileum prepares chyme for the large intestine. Together they measure more than 20 feet on average.

options.t: Jejunum receives chyme; ileum absorbs water
options.why: The duodenum receives chyme from the stomach.

options.t: Both perform identical absorptive work
options.why: They have distinct roles.

options.t: Jejunum preps for the colon; ileum absorbs
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Jejunum absorbs; ileum preps for the colon

questions.stem: How long is the large intestine, and what is its main role?
questions.why: The large intestine is about 5 feet long, encircling the outer border of the abdomen around the small intestine. Its main role is completing the reabsorption of water, and its osmotic function helps solidify the stool.

options.t: About 20 feet; it absorbs nutrients
options.why: That is the small intestine's length and role.

options.t: About 10 feet; it secretes enzymes
options.why: That overstates its length.

options.t: About 5 feet; it reabsorbs water
About 5 feet; it digests proteins
options.why: Protein digestion happens in the small intestine.

questions.stem: What are the three components of the large intestine?
questions.why: Cecum, colon, and rectum. Feces travel through the descending colon, then the sigmoid colon, then the rectum, which joins the anal canal.

options.t: Cecum, appendix, and sigmoid
options.why: The appendix and sigmoid are parts within those regions.

options.t: Cecum, colon, and rectum
Ascending, transverse, and descending colon
options.why: Those are subdivisions of the colon only.

options.t: Duodenum, jejunum, and ileum
options.why: Those are the small intestine's divisions.

questions.stem: What do intestinal flora do in the large intestine?
questions.why: Intestinal flora — normal bacteria — break down some of the molecules that have not been digested.

options.t: Break down some of the molecules that have not been digested
Trigger the peristaltic waves that move contents to the rectum
options.why: Peristalsis is driven by the muscular layer.

options.t: Produce the enzymes that finish protein digestion
options.why: Digestive enzymes come from the pancreas and intestine.

options.t: Reabsorb water from the digestive contents
options.why: That is the large intestine's own function.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the internal and external anal sphincters?
questions.why: Internal sphincter: autonomic, with the stretch receptors producing the urge. External sphincter: voluntary, allowing a controlled bowel movement.

options.t: Internal is autonomic; external is voluntary
Both are voluntary, with stretch receptors
options.why: The internal sphincter is autonomic.

options.t: Both are autonomic, at differing pressures
options.why: The external sphincter is voluntary.

options.t: Internal is voluntary; external is autonomic
options.why: The two are reversed here.

questions.stem: How often do peristaltic waves occur in the large intestine, and what typically triggers the mass movements?
questions.why: Large intestine peristaltic waves happen only two to three times per day. The intestinal walls constrict vigorously — mass movements — forcing contents toward the rectum, usually following a meal but sometimes from mucosal irritation.

options.t: Continuously, driven by water reabsorption
options.why: Large intestine waves are infrequent, not continuous.

options.t: Hourly, triggered by the release of bile
options.why: Bile release is unrelated to colonic mass movement.

options.t: Two or three a day, usually after meals
Once daily, triggered by voluntary effort
options.why: They occur two or three times daily.

questions.stem: How does the liver detoxify the blood?
questions.why: The liver detoxifies the blood by converting ammonia into urea. Its other major functions are maintaining blood glucose through glycogen stores, manufacturing plasma proteins and clotting factors, and regulating fats.

options.t: By binding toxins to plasma proteins for storage
options.why: Toxins are converted rather than stored.

options.t: By converting ammonia to urea
By filtering nitrogenous waste into bile for excretion
options.why: The kidneys filter nitrogen waste.

options.t: By converting urea to ammonia
options.why: The conversion runs ammonia to urea.

questions.stem: What proportion of the body's blood circulates through the liver, and why does that matter?
questions.why: The liver is a highly vascular organ through which 100% of the body's blood circulates. That is what allows detoxification of all nutrients absorbed from the intestinal tract, delivered by vessels of the portal vein, before release into the general venous circulation.

options.t: About a quarter, filtering most toxins
options.why: All of the body's blood passes through.

options.t: About half, the rest bypassing the liver
options.why: None of it bypasses the liver.

options.t: All of it, so everything gets detoxified
About a tenth, mostly processing stores
options.why: That greatly understates hepatic blood flow.

questions.stem: What happens to old red blood cells in the liver, and what is the yellow byproduct?
questions.why: Old RBCs enter the liver and are broken down into bile, which breaks down fats. Bilirubin, a yellow compound, is a byproduct and is usually excreted in the feces — which is why liver dysfunction produces jaundice.

options.t: Recycled into new cells; ammonia becomes urea
options.why: Ammonia to urea is detoxification, a separate process.

options.t: Broken into bile; bilirubin leaves in feces
Broken into plasma proteins; urea in urine
options.why: Plasma proteins are made, not derived from red cells.

options.t: Converted to glycogen; bile stored in the sac
options.why: Bile comes from red cell breakdown, not glycogen.

questions.stem: What is the gallbladder, and what is its function?
questions.why: The gallbladder is an outpouching from the bile ducts. It serves as a reservoir and concentrating organ for bile — but the liver is what produces the bile.

options.t: A gland manufacturing bile from cholesterol
options.why: The liver manufactures bile; the gallbladder stores it.

options.t: A second filter for blood leaving the liver
options.why: The liver itself processes the blood.

options.t: A pouch storing and concentrating bile
A valve controlling chyme into the duodenum
options.why: That is the pyloric sphincter.

questions.stem: What triggers the gallbladder to contract and empty, and through which duct does it discharge?
questions.why: Food in the duodenum triggers gallbladder contraction, and the gallbladder discharges bile into the duodenum through the common bile duct. The liver connects to the common bile duct via the hepatic duct.

options.t: The release of insulin from the pancreas; it discharges through the pancreatic duct
options.why: Insulin governs glucose, not bile release.

options.t: Rising blood bilirubin levels; it discharges through the sphincter of Oddi
options.why: Bilirubin is a byproduct, not a trigger.

options.t: The presence of food in the duodenum; it discharges through the common bile duct
The presence of food in the stomach; it discharges through the hepatic duct
options.why: Food must reach the duodenum to trigger release.

questions.stem: What is the function of the sphincter of Oddi?
questions.why: The sphincter of Oddi sits at the end of the bile duct and regulates the movement of bile into the duodenum. The bile ducts and gallbladder together form the biliary system.

options.t: Prevents reflux back into the gallbladder
options.why: It regulates outflow rather than preventing reflux.

options.t: Controls chyme flow into the duodenum
options.why: That is the pyloric sphincter.

options.t: Controls bile flow into the duodenum
Controls enzyme release into the stomach
options.why: Pancreatic enzymes enter the duodenum, not the stomach.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the pancreas's endocrine functions?
questions.why: Endocrine means released into the blood: glucagon, insulin, and somatostatin. Glucagon and insulin are critical to maintaining blood glucose, and somatostatin works as a negative feedback system.

options.t: Production of pancreatic digestive juices released through the pancreatic duct
options.why: That is the exocrine function.

options.t: Storage and concentration of bile produced by the liver
options.why: That is the gallbladder's role.

options.t: Conversion of ammonia to urea
options.why: That is a liver function.

options.t: Synthesis of glucagon, insulin, and somatostatin, released into the blood

questions.stem: The exocrine function of the pancreas involves what?
questions.why: Exocrine means NOT into the bloodstream. The pancreas produces digestive juices and releases them through the pancreatic duct into the duodenum.

options.t: Storage of bile made by the liver
options.why: That is the gallbladder's role.

options.t: Insulin and glucagon into the blood
options.why: That is the endocrine function.

options.t: Digestive juices into the duodenum
Absorption of nutrients from chyme
options.why: Absorption happens in the intestinal wall.

questions.stem: What is the path of the products of digestion after they cross the intestinal wall?
questions.why: Products of digestion cross the intestinal wall, travel through the portal vein to the liver, are processed and stored or sent to the heart via veins draining the liver, and are then pumped through the arteries to the capillaries where they nourish cells.

options.t: Into lymph, then heart, then arteries
options.why: Most nutrients travel by vein, not lymph.

options.t: Straight into arteries, bypassing the liver
options.why: Absorbed nutrients pass through the liver first.

options.t: Portal vein, liver, heart, arteries
Hepatic artery, heart, back to the gut
options.why: The hepatic artery supplies the liver rather than draining it.

questions.stem: What is metabolism, and what is basal metabolic rate?
questions.why: Metabolism is the sum of all chemical and biological reactions of an organism, and also describes the rate at which the body processes food. Basal metabolic rate is the rate at which nutrients are consumed.

options.t: Breakdown in the stomach; the speed of it
options.why: Metabolism covers all reactions, not just gastric breakdown.

options.t: Absorption of nutrients; the rate of uptake
options.why: Absorption moves nutrients rather than transforming them.

options.t: All chemical reactions; the rate of use
Storage of excess; the rate of fat gain
options.why: Storage is one outcome of metabolism.

questions.stem: What are the two most common ways the body obtains nutrients?
questions.why: Inhalation for oxygen and ingestion for food. Oxygen counts as a nutrient in this framework.

options.t: Ingestion for food and absorption through the skin
options.why: Skin absorption is not a main nutrient route.

options.t: Inhalation for oxygen and ingestion for food
Ingestion for food and osmosis from interstitial fluid
options.why: Osmosis moves water rather than supplying nutrients.

options.t: Inhalation for oxygen and injection for medication
options.why: Injection is not one of the two common routes.

questions.stem: What is the difference between macronutrients and micronutrients?
questions.why: Macronutrients — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins — are needed in large amounts and provide energy. Micronutrients — vitamins and minerals — are needed in much smaller amounts and enable the biochemical reactions that extract energy from macronutrients.

options.t: Macro can be stored; micro cannot be
options.why: Both can be stored in some form.

options.t: Macro are vitamins; micro are carbohydrates
options.why: Vitamins are micronutrients.

options.t: Macro enable reactions; micro give energy
options.why: The two are reversed here.

options.t: Macro give energy; micro enable reactions

questions.stem: How many calories does one gram of each macronutrient yield?
questions.why: Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9. A calorie is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a gram of water by 1°C — and fat carries more than double the energy density of the other two.

options.t: Carbohydrate about 9, protein about 4, fat about 4
options.why: Carbohydrate yields 4, not 9.

options.t: Carbohydrate about 4, protein about 4, fat about 9
Carbohydrate about 4, protein about 9, fat about 4
options.why: Protein yields 4, not 9.

options.t: All three yield about 4 calories per gram
options.why: Fat yields more than the other two.

questions.stem: What happens when the amount of nutrients and energy the body consumes exceeds what is available in the diet?
questions.why: If the body's demand outstrips the diet, body structures may be metabolized to sustain life. Going the other way, surplus nutrients are stored (lipids, for example) or excreted through waste.

options.t: Body structures may be metabolized to sustain life
Stored lipids are converted directly into protein
options.why: Lipids are not converted into protein.

options.t: Metabolism slows until intake resumes
options.why: Body structures are metabolized rather than metabolism halting.

options.t: Excess nutrients are excreted through elimination of waste
options.why: Excretion handles surplus, not deficit.

questions.stem: Digestion breaks carbohydrates down into which molecules, and what happens to two of them?
questions.why: Carbohydrates break down into monosaccharides — fructose, galactose, and glucose — for easy absorption. Liver enzymes convert fructose and galactose to glucose, the form most commonly oxidized as cellular fuel.

options.t: Monosaccharides; the liver converts two
Fatty acids; the liver converts to glucose
options.why: Fatty acids come from fat digestion.

options.t: Disaccharides; the liver makes glycogen
options.why: Disaccharides must be broken down further.

options.t: Amino acids; the liver converts to glucose
options.why: Amino acids come from protein digestion.

questions.stem: Which cell type requires continuous glucose to survive, and what happens when carbohydrate intake is insufficient?
questions.why: Many cells get energy by oxidizing fatty acids, but neurons require continuous glucose to survive. When carbohydrates are not sufficiently consumed, the liver may convert amino acids from proteins into glucose.

options.t: Red cells; the kidney makes it from bilirubin
options.why: Red cells use glucose but neurons are the named example.

options.t: Muscle cells; the liver converts stored fat
options.why: Muscle cells can burn fatty acids instead.

options.t: Neurons; the liver converts amino acids
Liver cells; the pancreas releases its stores
options.why: The liver supplies glucose rather than requiring it continuously.

questions.stem: In what order does the body metabolize fuel sources for energy?
questions.why: Glucose, then glycogen back into glucose, then fats and proteins. Excess glucose becomes glycogen stored in liver and muscles — which can be rapidly mobilized, but only a certain amount can be stored, so further excess converts to fat in adipose tissue.

options.t: Protein first, then glucose, then fat
options.why: Protein is the last resort, not the first.

options.t: Fat first, then glycogen, then glucose
options.why: Glucose is used first, not fat.

options.t: Glycogen first, then fat, then glucose
options.why: Free glucose is consumed before glycogen.

options.t: Glucose, then glycogen, then fat and protein

questions.stem: Match each digestive process to its definition.
questions.why: Six processes in order from mouth to exit. Mechanical processing is physical and digestion is chemical — the pair most often confused.
pairs: Materials enter the digestive tract via the mouth
Materials are crushed and broken into smaller fragments
Chemical breakdown of food into particles small enough to absorb
Release of water, acids, buffers, enzymes, and salts into the tract
Movement of substrates and water across the epithelium into interstitial fluid
Removal of waste products mixed with indigestible residue

questions.stem: Match each abdominal quadrant to the organs it contains.
questions.why: Liver and gallbladder on the right, stomach and spleen on the left, appendix in the RLQ. Some organs cross into more than one quadrant.
pairs: Liver, gallbladder, some colon and small intestine
Stomach, spleen, some colon and small intestine
Descending and sigmoid parts of the colon

questions.stem: Match each digestive structure to its defining function.
questions.why: Absorption happens almost entirely in the small intestine — over 90% of it. The esophagus only transports, and the large intestine mostly handles water.
pairs: Transports food by peristalsis; cannot absorb nutrients
Receives and stores food, converting it into chyme
Receives chyme; connects pancreas, liver, and gallbladder to the tract
Completes the reabsorption of water and solidifies stool
Reservoir and concentrating organ for bile made in the liver
